For a number in a table, use type.body. Don't use a small or mono font. Every number must be readable at large size.

When no component in the inventory fits, use a native HTML element with a label and a hint. Don't use a custom widget that needs hover, drag or precise pointing. Native elements work with every assistive technology without extra work.

For a field label or column header, use type.label, above the field, always visible. Don't use a placeholder as the label. Labels must stay visible while typing.
For a link, use color.text.link, underlined. Don't use color only. Underline works without color perception.
For keyboard focus, use button/focus-ring at border-width.focus, with an offset. Don't use a thin or faint outline. Focus must be seen by everyone.
Button's danger variant. The confirm of a delete, always with the verb and an icon, so color is never the only cue.
Button's focus state. Seen by everyone: the focus ring with an offset.
Button's disabled state isn't used. Keep it enabled and explain on press: nobody is left out, and nobody remembers the interface from last time.
Field's vertical orientation. Every question: the label above the field, always visible.
Field's horizontal orientation isn't used. Labels stay above the field, visible while typing and in the same place on any screen.
Input group's inline-start align. A currency sign before the amount, with the label still above the field.
Input group's inline-end align. A unit after the value, as a word people can read, with the label still above the field.
Input group's block-start align isn't used. The label stays above the field, outside it, always visible.
Input group's block-end align isn't used. Hints and errors sit in the field layout, in the same place on every question.

For a page title, use type.title. Don't use type.display. The same title size on every page tells people where they are. The display size changes from page to page and pushes the content down.
For a paragraph or help text, use type.body, short sentences. Don't use type.caption. Large text and short lines lower effort.
For a first visit, use say how many steps there are and how long it takes. Don't use marketing copy. Knowing the length lowers effort and anxiety.
Alert's default variant. Important notes that stay on the page while people answer.
Empty's default variant isn't used. The brand stays out of the way: words say what will appear and how to start.

items.text: Iconography · What do icons do? → Actions and status
For an alternative or cancel, use button secondary. Don't use a text link. Every action looks like a button people can find.
For an action on one row or item, use button secondary with a word. Don't use an icon on its own. A word says what will happen.
Button's secondary variant. Every other action, always with a word: alternatives, row actions, and the first step of a delete.
Button's ghost variant isn't used. Every action looks like a button people can find.
Button's disabled state isn't used. Keep it enabled and explain on press: nobody is left out, and nobody remembers the interface from last time.
Field's responsive orientation isn't used. One layout on every device, so people meet the same form every time.
Toggle's default variant isn't used. Every action looks like a control people can find, so the toggle keeps its border.

outcomes-q1.why: Completion without errors is the measure.
because: What is the main task? → Complete a form

items.text: Color · Where does color carry meaning first? → Links and actions
Voice and tone · Where do the words matter most? → Form steps and errors
For a success message, use confirm what happened and what comes next. Don't use a confirmation with no next step. People need to know the task is finished and what happens now.
Alert's default variant. Important notes that stay on the page while people answer.
Badge's success tone. A finished task, with a filled icon and a word.

outcomes-q2.why: A failed form can cost someone a benefit.
because: What is the main task? → Complete a form

items.text: For an error message, use color.status.danger, an icon and a sentence next to the field. Don't use color alone. People must know what went wrong and where.
For a delete or remove, use button secondary, then a confirm page with Button danger. Don't use button primary. A confirm step prevents a costly error.
For a confirmation question, use say what will happen in plain words, and offer a way back. Don't use a double negative. Plain words prevent a choice people did not mean.
Button's secondary variant. Every other action, always with a word: alternatives, row actions, and the first step of a delete.
Button's danger variant. The confirm of a delete, always with the verb and an icon, so color is never the only cue.
Alert's destructive variant. Errors, with what went wrong, where, and exactly how to fix it, next to the field.
Badge's warning tone. A risk people can still fix before they finish, with an icon and a word.
Badge's danger tone. A failure that blocks the task, with a filled icon and a word; an alert says how to fix it.

brand-q3.why: Atkinson Hyperlegible for everything: it was drawn so letters can't be mistaken, and nobody is left out.

items.label: Readability
items.text: Atkinson Hyperlegible was designed by the Braille Institute for readers with low vision.

items.label: Legibility
items.text: Its letters are drawn to stay apart: I, l and 1, 0 and O, b and d don't look alike.

items.label: Scalability
items.text: Regular and bold carry the hierarchy; size does the rest, so every role stays readable.

items.label: Numerals
items.text: Its digits are drawn to be told apart; figures line up when columns align to the right.

items.label: Scripts and languages
items.text: Latin, with accents for many languages; other scripts need a face chosen for the same legibility.

items.label: Recognition
items.text: Accessibility is the brand promise, and the face says it.

items.label: Familiarity
items.text: A plain, open sans feels familiar and calm in forms and steps.

items.label: Personality
items.text: Calm and clear, never clever, as the brand answer asks.

items.label: Performance
items.text: One family, two weights: the lightest load of all five schemes.

items.label: Licensing
items.text: SIL Open Font License: free to embed in apps and on the web.

items.label: Fallback and pairing
items.text: Falls back to Verdana, a wide, legible system face, as its token says; no second face is needed.

items.text: For a button label, use a common verb that says what happens next. Don't use "Submit" or "Proceed". Common words are understood by the most people.
For the words of an error, use say what is wrong, where, and exactly how to fix it. Don't use "Invalid input". People must be able to fix the error without help.

For a confirmation question, use say what will happen in plain words, and offer a way back. Don't use a double negative. Plain words prevent a choice people did not mean.
